subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Yemen's Coffee Monopoly
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Yemen's Coffee Monopoly.

hook.text: For nearly 200 years, Yemen was the world's only source of cultivated coffee beans.

buildup.text: Farmers grew coffee on steep, terraced hillsides irrigated by ancient canal systems.

discovery.text: To protect the monopoly, Yemen required all exported beans to be boiled or sun-dried until infertile.

twist.text: Around 1600, a pilgrim named Baba Budan smuggled seven fertile beans out, strapped to his body.

climax.text: Those seeds reached India, then the Dutch took plants to Java. Yemen's monopoly crumbled.

punchline.text: Seven smuggled beans broke a 200-year monopoly.

quiz.question: How did Yemen try to protect its coffee monopoly?
options: Exporting only boiled or sun-dried infertile beans

details.summary: For nearly two centuries, Yemen controlled the world's entire supply of cultivated coffee. The port of Mocha on the Red Sea was the only commercial outlet. European demand made coffee enormously valuable, and Yemen fiercely guarded its monopoly by banning the export of fertile seeds.
details.whyItMatters: Yemen's monopoly made coffee one of the world's first globally traded luxury commodities and set the stage for the colonial coffee plantations that followed its collapse.
takeaways: Yemen monopolized global coffee supply for nearly 200 years
The port of Mocha was the sole commercial export hub
Fertile seeds were banned from export to protect the monopoly

faq.question: How did the name Mocha become associated with coffee?
faq.answer: The port of Mocha in Yemen was the primary shipping point for all coffee leaving Arabia. European buyers associated the port name with the product. Over time, mocha came to describe both a type of coffee bean and the chocolate-coffee flavor combination inspired by Yemen's distinctive earthy beans.

faq.question: What ended Yemen's coffee monopoly?
faq.answer: The Dutch East India Company smuggled a coffee plant out of Yemen around 1616 and established plantations in Java. The French took cuttings to their colonies. Once coffee grew outside Yemen, the monopoly collapsed. Yemen's share of global production shrank rapidly through the 1700s.
